nodes.title: TAXONOMY
nodes.body:
Common Name:  Gray Snapper
Scientific Name:  Lutjanus griseus

nodes.title: Classification
nodes.body:
Phylum: Chordata
	Class: Osteichthyes
	Order: Perciformes
	Family: Lutjanidae

Other Common Names:  Mangrove snapper (312 581 664 834 887 932); grey snapper (1389); mango snapper, black snapper (60).

nodes.title: VALUE & STATUS
nodes.body:
Commercial:  An important food fish in southeast Florida, the West Indies and Panama (312).  Caught with beach seines, boat seines, gill nets, hook and line (Rutherford et al. 1989), and traps (791).  In Florida, they are caught mainly by hook and line with cut bait (60).  Approximately 588,820 lbs., worth $816,487 were landed in Florida during 1989 (902).  They are mostly marketed fresh and are excellent eating (791).  Sometimes marketed as ‘red snapper’ (788).
Recreational:  This species forms a major portion of the sport catch in south Florida and is highly sought for food (60).  Recreational catch for Florida was estimated as 2,440,000 fish caught during 1990 (1363).  One of the most commonly caught sport fish in southwest Florida (1373).
Ecological: Harrigan et al. (1989) determined that within a mangrove and seagrass system carbon and nitrogen are transferred from a detrital base to the grey snapper by similar mechanisms.

nodes.title: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
nodes.body:
Overall:  Western Atlantic, tropical and subtropical marine and estuarine waters of Florida, the West Indies, Bermuda, the Bahamas, and the shelf waters of the Gulf of Mexico.  Occasionally juveniles are found as far north as Cape Cod, Massachusetts and as far south as Rio de Janeiro, Brazil (60 788 791 891).

Within Study Area:  Found throughout Florida waters (60 788 791 887 891).  Very common off southeast Florida (791).  Caught in considerable quantities in the Tampa Bay area (664), and one of the most abundant snapper in Indian River Lagoon (887 993).

nodes.title: Life Mode
nodes.body:
Eggs: eggs are planktonic and occur offshore (60).
Larvae: larvae are planktonic and occur offshore (60).
Juveniles: juveniles are pelagic and non-schooling in early stages; larger juveniles are weak schoolers (363).
Adults: Adults are pelagic and demersal, often in schools diurnally, dispersing by night (153 481).

nodes.title: Movements/Migrations
nodes.body: The adults tend to remain in areas in which they have become established except for seasonal, inshore to reef spawning migrations (672).  Mature fish migrate to offshore reefs during the summer to spawn(672).  Most return to the inland habitats, however some remain near the reefs (672).  Adults that inhabit reefs move off into surrounding waters to feed at night (671 481).  Newly hatched larvae are planktonic but develop rapidly and make their way to the inshore nursery areas at about 10 mm (672).  There is some evidence of limited inshore movements (38 887 1389), with a maximum distance travelled of 122km in 106 days in the Indian River Lagoon (887).

nodes.title: Habitat Type
nodes.body:
Eggs: eggs are marine, neritic demersal (1363);
Larvae: larvae are marine, neritic planktonic (60).
Juvenile: juveniles are estuarine, riverine and marine; found in estuaries, mangrove swamps, freshwater creeks, and in later stages some move to offshore habitats with adults (312 581 790 871 932 1389).
Adults: adults are marine, estuarine and riverine, occurring offshore near coral reefs, rock shelves and similar situations; inshore near ledges of channels and around artificial structures; in estuaries, mangrove swamps and lagoons; ascending freshwater creeks and rivers, even reported from some freshwater lakes (153 312 254 790 935 1389).  Fish have been reported from depths of 77 m (1222).

nodes.title: Substrate
nodes.body:
Egg: eggs occur in the vicinity of offshore reefs (1389). Powell et al. (568) noted pre-flexion gray snappers ‘candidates’ over offshore reefs.  Lutjanidae larvae reported from shelf water from Florida to Texas (802).
Juvenile: juveniles are recorded from Thalassia grass flats; soft marl bottoms, marl sands, fine marl mud with shell and rock outcrops, and detritus; seagrass meadows and mangrove roots; seagrass meadows near jetties and pilings; postlarval juveniles have been found over dense (1000-4000 shoots/m^2) seagrass beds of Halodule wrightii and Syringodium filiforme; postflexion larvae and juveniles (15-35 mm) present in shallow basins with Thalassia present adjacent to mud banks (60 153 312 671 873 1433).
Adult: adults typically occur around hard bottoms, natural and artificial, but also soft bottoms; wharves, pilings, rocky areas; sand, rubble, rock with supporting alcyonarians, sponges and Thalassia; coral reefs, rock outcrops, shipwrecks; sandy grass beds, coral reefs, sandy, muddy and rocky bottoms, and marl (153 378 481 664 671 672 833 892 932 1384).

nodes.title: Physical/Chemical
nodes.body:
Temperature: Temperature ranges of some Florida collections include: 17.2-33.0 C at Cedar Key (378 581); 13.4-32.5 C at Tampa Bay (664); 16-31 C at Everglades National Park (702 1373); 19.9-33.6 C at Matecumbe Key (800); and 16-39+ C at Jupiter Inlet (887).  Reported by several authors to be killed by low water temperatures caused by freezes (232 236 672 702 836 997 1068).
Larvae: larvae have been recorded in ranges of 15.6-27.2 C (275); 26-28 C in vitro (594).
Juvenile: juveniles recorded in ranges 17.2-36.0 C (275); 16-31 C (702).  Lower lethal temperature limit 11-14 C (672).

nodes.title: Salinity
nodes.body:
Egg: eggs marine seawater zone; spawning occurs in the vicinity of offshore reefs (672).
Larvae are euryhaline; range not reported, but known offshore shelf waters and near coral reefs; pre-juveniles begin to move into estuarine habitats (672 593 275).  32 - 36 in vitro (594).
Juvenile: juveniles are euryhaline, reported range 0 - 37 ppt (702 60 612).
Adult: adults are euryhaline ranging from 0 - 47.7 ppt (153 275 891).  Representative Florida collections include: 3.9 - 25.9 % at Cedar Key (378 581); 3-35 % at Tampa Bay (664); 26.5-35 % in the Caloosahatchee River (265); 0-43.3 % in Everglades National Park (702 790 1373); 34.5-37.9 % at Matecumbe Key (800); and 1-36.6 %in the Indian River Lagoon (887).  Probably occur in most river systems in southern Florida, and in large drainage canals without salinity barriers (790).

nodes.title: REPRODUCTION
nodes.body:
Reproductive Mode:  Reproduction is sexual.  Gray snapper are dioecious, exhibiting no apparent external dimorphism.  Sex ratio is reported as equal in Florida (154 672 612), but a 2:1 female to male sex ratio has been reported off Cuba (1273).  Fertilization is by means of externally broadcast sexual products (672 244), with no indication of nest building or egg guarding.

Mating/Spawning: Gray snapper are summer spawners, typically from June through August but also reported in September in the Florida keys (672 244). Spawning occurs offshore (244 664 672).  Evidence indicates batch spawning occurs at night near full moons throughout the reproductive cycle (672 244).

Fecundity: Fecundity has been reported as 1.25 X 10^5 eggs/g ovarian tissue (672). Fecundity estimates range from 548,000 eggs for a 354mm SL female and 590,000 eggs for a 315mm SL fish (672), to 1.1-5.9 million eggs/female for fish 488-600mm TL (1273).  Equations expressing the fecundity to length and weight relationship have been calculated (1273) as:
[eq]
     F = 0.00299 x TL^3.26, TL in mm
     F = 1478.82 x W^0,973 W in gms
[/eq]

Development: Embryonic Development; Oviparous.

nodes.title: Length Range
nodes.body:
Eggs:  The eggs are non-adhesive, ranging from 0.04 - 0.06 mm in diameter and contain a single central oil globule (672 244).  The demersal eggs develop rapidly and hatch in about 18 h in ambient seawater (244).  Eggs hatch in the vicinity of offshore reefs.
Larvae: Larval development takes place offshore near spawning site (593 568).  Newly hatched larvae absorb their yolk sac within 45 h (244).  Richards and Saksena (1980) gave growth rates continually fed larvae as 2.7-2.8 mm NL (4 days), 3.0-3.1 mm NL (5 days), 3.4 mm NL (7 days), 4.1-4.2 mm NL (9 days), 6.2 mm SL (15 days), 9.6-12.5 mm SL (26 days) and 15.4 mm SL (36 days).  Flexion occurs about 4.2 mm SL, post-flexion at 6.2 mm SL and juveniles are identifiable at 12 mm SL.  Larvae are sparsely pigmented; juveniles are heavily pigmented and can be identified by full complement of meristic characters (594).
Juveniles:  Same as Larval growth
Adult: Springer and Woodburn (664) reported mean lengths of first year ‘0’ class fish for periods of September, November and December 1957 as 33 mm, 42.6 mm and 51.7 mm respectfully.  The following year they gave ‘0’ class lengths for October (18.2 mm), November (25.3 mm) and December (34 mm),  Croker (154) back calculated mean FL for age classes I-VII as 81 mm, 180 mm. 241 mm, 295 mm, 352 mm, 431 mm and 456 mm.  The work by Starck and Schroeder (672), did not completely agree, particularly in the later age classes: I - 79 mm, II - 143 mm, III - 199 mm, IV - 255 mm, V - 293 mm, VI - 334 mm, VII - 381 mm, VIII - 438 mm, and IX - 478 mm.  Growth rates of 126 +/- 2 mm for the first year and 48-62 mm/y for fish one to four years of age was given by Rutherford et al. (612).  Using sectioned otoliths, Manooch and Matheson (1390) calculated TL for fish up to 19 years of age.   A length of 772 mm was determined for 19 year old fish.  The oldest specimen they observed was a 775 mm fish, 21 years old.  Length/weight equations have not been calculated (60).  Records of fish larger than 600mm are questionable and may be based on Cubera snapper (788).  Starck and Schroeder (672) suggest maximum weight for the gray snapper at around 8 kg but stated that fish of 3.6 kg were rare.  Maturity is reached at about 200 mm TL, probably during the third year (672).

nodes.title: FOOD HABITS
nodes.body:
Gray snapper are carnivorous at all life stages.
In vitro: Richards and Saksena (594) fed newly hatched larvae zooplankton in the 73 - 110um range.  Copepods and amphipods are important food items of fish at 10 - 20 mm (664 672).
Juvenile: juveniles are diurnal feeders that primarily prey on crustaceans, but they also consume fish, molluscs and polychaetes (672).
Adult: adults are typically nocturnal predators, consuming mostly fish, but also taking shrimp and crabs (154 671 837).  Fish eaten are largely grunts of the genus Haemulon.  Algae and marine plants are commonly found, possibly consumed accidentally during routine feeding.  Proportions of prey species consumed varies within particular biotopes inhabited (581 664 702 671 672 612).

sections.heading: HEADER
sections.content:
Title:  Gray snapper (Lutjanus griseus)

FLELMR Code:  1659

sections.heading: Revisions
sections.content:
1993.  T.D Philipps; Mote Marine Laboratory, Sarasota, Florida.
4/4/1994.  Steve Traxler; Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institution, Florida.

sections.heading: TAXONOMY
sections.content:
Common Name:  Gray Snapper
Scientific Name:  Lutjanus griseus

sections.heading: Classification
sections.content:
Phylum: Chordata
	Class: Osteichthyes
	Order: Perciformes
	Family: Lutjanidae

Other Common Names:  Mangrove snapper (312 581 664 834 887 932); grey snapper (1389); mango snapper, black snapper (60).

sections.heading: VALUE & STATUS
sections.content:
Commercial:  An important food fish in southeast Florida, the West Indies and Panama (312).  Caught with beach seines, boat seines, gill nets, hook and line (Rutherford et al. 1989), and traps (791).  In Florida, they are caught mainly by hook and line with cut bait (60).  Approximately 588,820 lbs., worth $816,487 were landed in Florida during 1989 (902).  They are mostly marketed fresh and are excellent eating (791).  Sometimes marketed as ‘red snapper’ (788).
Recreational:  This species forms a major portion of the sport catch in south Florida and is highly sought for food (60).  Recreational catch for Florida was estimated as 2,440,000 fish caught during 1990 (1363).  One of the most commonly caught sport fish in southwest Florida (1373).
Ecological: Harrigan et al. (1989) determined that within a mangrove and seagrass system carbon and nitrogen are transferred from a detrital base to the grey snapper by similar mechanisms.

sections.heading: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
sections.content:
Overall:  Western Atlantic, tropical and subtropical marine and estuarine waters of Florida, the West Indies, Bermuda, the Bahamas, and the shelf waters of the Gulf of Mexico.  Occasionally juveniles are found as far north as Cape Cod, Massachusetts and as far south as Rio de Janeiro, Brazil (60 788 791 891).

Within Study Area:  Found throughout Florida waters (60 788 791 887 891).  Very common off southeast Florida (791).  Caught in considerable quantities in the Tampa Bay area (664), and one of the most abundant snapper in Indian River Lagoon (887 993).

sections.heading: Life Mode
sections.content:
Eggs: eggs are planktonic and occur offshore (60).
Larvae: larvae are planktonic and occur offshore (60).
Juveniles: juveniles are pelagic and non-schooling in early stages; larger juveniles are weak schoolers (363).
Adults: Adults are pelagic and demersal, often in schools diurnally, dispersing by night (153 481).

sections.heading: Movements/Migrations
sections.content: The adults tend to remain in areas in which they have become established except for seasonal, inshore to reef spawning migrations (672).  Mature fish migrate to offshore reefs during the summer to spawn(672).  Most return to the inland habitats, however some remain near the reefs (672).  Adults that inhabit reefs move off into surrounding waters to feed at night (671 481).  Newly hatched larvae are planktonic but develop rapidly and make their way to the inshore nursery areas at about 10 mm (672).  There is some evidence of limited inshore movements (38 887 1389), with a maximum distance travelled of 122km in 106 days in the Indian River Lagoon (887).

sections.heading: Habitat Type
sections.content:
Eggs: eggs are marine, neritic demersal (1363);
Larvae: larvae are marine, neritic planktonic (60).
Juvenile: juveniles are estuarine, riverine and marine; found in estuaries, mangrove swamps, freshwater creeks, and in later stages some move to offshore habitats with adults (312 581 790 871 932 1389).
Adults: adults are marine, estuarine and riverine, occurring offshore near coral reefs, rock shelves and similar situations; inshore near ledges of channels and around artificial structures; in estuaries, mangrove swamps and lagoons; ascending freshwater creeks and rivers, even reported from some freshwater lakes (153 312 254 790 935 1389).  Fish have been reported from depths of 77 m (1222).

sections.heading: Substrate
sections.content:
Egg: eggs occur in the vicinity of offshore reefs (1389). Powell et al. (568) noted pre-flexion gray snappers ‘candidates’ over offshore reefs.  Lutjanidae larvae reported from shelf water from Florida to Texas (802).
Juvenile: juveniles are recorded from Thalassia grass flats; soft marl bottoms, marl sands, fine marl mud with shell and rock outcrops, and detritus; seagrass meadows and mangrove roots; seagrass meadows near jetties and pilings; postlarval juveniles have been found over dense (1000-4000 shoots/m^2) seagrass beds of Halodule wrightii and Syringodium filiforme; postflexion larvae and juveniles (15-35 mm) present in shallow basins with Thalassia present adjacent to mud banks (60 153 312 671 873 1433).
Adult: adults typically occur around hard bottoms, natural and artificial, but also soft bottoms; wharves, pilings, rocky areas; sand, rubble, rock with supporting alcyonarians, sponges and Thalassia; coral reefs, rock outcrops, shipwrecks; sandy grass beds, coral reefs, sandy, muddy and rocky bottoms, and marl (153 378 481 664 671 672 833 892 932 1384).

sections.heading: Physical/Chemical
sections.content:
Temperature: Temperature ranges of some Florida collections include: 17.2-33.0 C at Cedar Key (378 581); 13.4-32.5 C at Tampa Bay (664); 16-31 C at Everglades National Park (702 1373); 19.9-33.6 C at Matecumbe Key (800); and 16-39+ C at Jupiter Inlet (887).  Reported by several authors to be killed by low water temperatures caused by freezes (232 236 672 702 836 997 1068).
Larvae: larvae have been recorded in ranges of 15.6-27.2 C (275); 26-28 C in vitro (594).
Juvenile: juveniles recorded in ranges 17.2-36.0 C (275); 16-31 C (702).  Lower lethal temperature limit 11-14 C (672).

sections.heading: Salinity
sections.content:
Egg: eggs marine seawater zone; spawning occurs in the vicinity of offshore reefs (672).
Larvae are euryhaline; range not reported, but known offshore shelf waters and near coral reefs; pre-juveniles begin to move into estuarine habitats (672 593 275).  32 - 36 in vitro (594).
Juvenile: juveniles are euryhaline, reported range 0 - 37 ppt (702 60 612).
Adult: adults are euryhaline ranging from 0 - 47.7 ppt (153 275 891).  Representative Florida collections include: 3.9 - 25.9 % at Cedar Key (378 581); 3-35 % at Tampa Bay (664); 26.5-35 % in the Caloosahatchee River (265); 0-43.3 % in Everglades National Park (702 790 1373); 34.5-37.9 % at Matecumbe Key (800); and 1-36.6 %in the Indian River Lagoon (887).  Probably occur in most river systems in southern Florida, and in large drainage canals without salinity barriers (790).

sections.heading: REPRODUCTION
sections.content:
Reproductive Mode:  Reproduction is sexual.  Gray snapper are dioecious, exhibiting no apparent external dimorphism.  Sex ratio is reported as equal in Florida (154 672 612), but a 2:1 female to male sex ratio has been reported off Cuba (1273).  Fertilization is by means of externally broadcast sexual products (672 244), with no indication of nest building or egg guarding.

Mating/Spawning: Gray snapper are summer spawners, typically from June through August but also reported in September in the Florida keys (672 244). Spawning occurs offshore (244 664 672).  Evidence indicates batch spawning occurs at night near full moons throughout the reproductive cycle (672 244).

Fecundity: Fecundity has been reported as 1.25 X 10^5 eggs/g ovarian tissue (672). Fecundity estimates range from 548,000 eggs for a 354mm SL female and 590,000 eggs for a 315mm SL fish (672), to 1.1-5.9 million eggs/female for fish 488-600mm TL (1273).  Equations expressing the fecundity to length and weight relationship have been calculated (1273) as:
[eq]
     F = 0.00299 x TL^3.26, TL in mm
     F = 1478.82 x W^0,973 W in gms
[/eq]

Development: Embryonic Development; Oviparous.

sections.heading: Length Range
sections.content:
Eggs:  The eggs are non-adhesive, ranging from 0.04 - 0.06 mm in diameter and contain a single central oil globule (672 244).  The demersal eggs develop rapidly and hatch in about 18 h in ambient seawater (244).  Eggs hatch in the vicinity of offshore reefs.
Larvae: Larval development takes place offshore near spawning site (593 568).  Newly hatched larvae absorb their yolk sac within 45 h (244).  Richards and Saksena (1980) gave growth rates continually fed larvae as 2.7-2.8 mm NL (4 days), 3.0-3.1 mm NL (5 days), 3.4 mm NL (7 days), 4.1-4.2 mm NL (9 days), 6.2 mm SL (15 days), 9.6-12.5 mm SL (26 days) and 15.4 mm SL (36 days).  Flexion occurs about 4.2 mm SL, post-flexion at 6.2 mm SL and juveniles are identifiable at 12 mm SL.  Larvae are sparsely pigmented; juveniles are heavily pigmented and can be identified by full complement of meristic characters (594).
Juveniles:  Same as Larval growth
Adult: Springer and Woodburn (664) reported mean lengths of first year ‘0’ class fish for periods of September, November and December 1957 as 33 mm, 42.6 mm and 51.7 mm respectfully.  The following year they gave ‘0’ class lengths for October (18.2 mm), November (25.3 mm) and December (34 mm),  Croker (154) back calculated mean FL for age classes I-VII as 81 mm, 180 mm. 241 mm, 295 mm, 352 mm, 431 mm and 456 mm.  The work by Starck and Schroeder (672), did not completely agree, particularly in the later age classes: I - 79 mm, II - 143 mm, III - 199 mm, IV - 255 mm, V - 293 mm, VI - 334 mm, VII - 381 mm, VIII - 438 mm, and IX - 478 mm.  Growth rates of 126 +/- 2 mm for the first year and 48-62 mm/y for fish one to four years of age was given by Rutherford et al. (612).  Using sectioned otoliths, Manooch and Matheson (1390) calculated TL for fish up to 19 years of age.   A length of 772 mm was determined for 19 year old fish.  The oldest specimen they observed was a 775 mm fish, 21 years old.  Length/weight equations have not been calculated (60).  Records of fish larger than 600mm are questionable and may be based on Cubera snapper (788).  Starck and Schroeder (672) suggest maximum weight for the gray snapper at around 8 kg but stated that fish of 3.6 kg were rare.  Maturity is reached at about 200 mm TL, probably during the third year (672).
